title: Shader source files (.gdshader) can be corrupted on system power loss: Propose an isolated cache mechanism like Unity's "Library" folder to protect source files
body: ### Tested versions - Reproducible in: Godot 4.X - Issue observed on: Windows 10 / Windows 11 ### System information Godot v4.6.stable.mono - Windows 10 (build 19045) - Multi-window, 2 monitors - OpenGL 3 (Compatibility) - NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 (NVIDIA; 32.0.15.8183) - 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-11400H @ 2.70GHz (12 threads) - 31.63 GiB memory ### Issue description When the operating system shuts down unexpectedly due to a power loss or similar event, the Godot engine can corrupt .gdshader source files in the user's project, even if those files were not being actively edited by the user at the time of the crash. The affected file becomes completely filled with hex 00 bytes, resulting in the permanent loss of the shader code unless recovered from an external backup or version control system. The root cause of this problem is that Godot's background processes (such as shader pre-compilation, hot-reloading, or the language server) perform direct file I/O operations (e.g., memory-mapped I/O) on the source files themselves, rather than operating on isolated cached copies. This direct handling exposes the original source files to the risk of file system corruption during an unexpected system interruption. **Comparison with the Unity Engine:** The Unity engine provides a more robust protection mechanism for source files through its Library folder. The Library folder acts as a comprehensive cache for the project. Unity's asset import pipeline transforms and stores all imported assets (textures, models, shaders, etc.) within this Library folder. At runtime, the engine relies entirely on the contents of this cache and does not touch the original source files located in the Assets folder. **This design offers a crucial advantage:** - Source File Safety: Original asset files are effectively treated as read-only by the engine; no background writes are performed on them. - Recoverability: If the Library cache folder becomes corrupted due to a crash or power loss, the developer can simply delete it. Unity will then automatically rebuild the entire cache from the pristine original source files on the next launch, ensuring the integrity and safety of the project's source code. I hadn't touched that shader in days. Why did it get corrupted when my laptop died? It should be read-only. The engine should never write to my source files without me hitting Save. It should load into a cache and do whatever it wants there. That way, even if it breaks, the original files are safe. I highlights a critical architectural shortcoming: Godot lacks a robust caching mechanism akin to Unity's **Library** folder to isolate and protect source files. Implementing such a mechanism would significantly enhance the engine's resilience against unexpected system interruptions. **Proposed Solution:** It is proposed to implement a similar, more isolated caching mechanism for Godot: 1. Confine all intermediate data and caches generated from importing, compiling, and hot-reloading operations strictly within the .godot folder (or a new, clearly structured cache folder). 2. Ensure that all background operations only read from source files and only write to the designated cache folder. 3. Rely exclusively on the cache folder during engine operation, thereby minimizing the risk exposure of the original source files. Godot 010Editor ### Steps to reproduce 1. Create a new Godot 4.x project. 2. Add a simple .gdshader file with valid shader code and save it. 3. Ensure the shader is assigned to a material and used in the main scene, so the engine has a reason to load and potentially interact with it in the background. 4. Let the editor sit idle for a while, simulating a normal workflow. 5 Simulate a sudden power loss: While the editor is open but the shader file is not being edited, forcefully terminate the Godot process (e.g., using "End Process Tree" in Task Manager on Windows, or kill -9 on Linux/macOS). 6. Reboot the system (or restart Godot) and inspect the .gdshader file with a hex editor or attempt to open it in Godot's shader editor. **Expected Result:** The file should remain intact and unchanged. **Actual Result:** With a certain low but non-zero probability, the file becomes corrupted and filled entirely with 00 bytes. ### Minimal reproduction project (MRP) N/A
